Sage.prep: Use sparingly as it is strong; fry whole leaves in butter until crisp to scatter over pasta or squash, or chop into stuffings and sausage meat.

Sorrel.about: Sorrel has bright green, spear-shaped leaves with a sharp, lemony tang. The young spring leaves are the most tender, which makes April and May its best months. A classic French sauce of sorrel, butter and cream is made for oily fish, and it also lifts soups and omelettes.
Sorrel.choose: Choose small to medium leaves that are crisp and bright green, avoiding large, tough or yellowing ones.
Sorrel.store: Wrap in damp kitchen paper in a bag in the fridge and use within two to three days, as it wilts fast.
Sorrel.prep: Shred young leaves raw into salads, or stir into butter, cream, soup or eggs at the last minute; it turns khaki when cooked, which is normal.

Tarragon.about: Tarragon has slender green leaves and a sweet, aniseed flavour that goes especially well with chicken, eggs and cream. Choose French tarragon for cooking, since Russian tarragon has a much weaker flavour. It is the main flavour in béarnaise sauce and grows well outdoors in UK summers.
Tarragon.choose: Buy French tarragon with glossy, aromatic leaves and no blackening; rub a leaf and it should smell clearly of aniseed.
Tarragon.store: Wrap in damp kitchen paper in the fridge and use within four or five days.
Tarragon.prep: Strip the leaves and chop just before using; stir into creamy sauces, dressings and mayonnaise or tuck under chicken skin before roasting.

Thyme.about: Thyme is a small, woody herb with tiny leaves and a warm, savoury flavour that holds up to long cooking. It grows in UK gardens all year, and alongside parsley and bay it makes up the classic bouquet garni for stocks, stews and braises. Lemon thyme is a milder, citrusy variety.
Thyme.choose: Choose bunches with fresh-smelling, grey-green leaves and pliable stems, avoiding any that are dry or mouldy.
Thyme.store: Wrap in damp kitchen paper in the fridge for up to two weeks, or hang to dry.
Thyme.prep: Strip the leaves by running your fingers down the stem against the direction of growth, or add whole sprigs to stews, roasts and stocks.

Wild garlic.about: Wild garlic, or ramsons, carpets damp woodland and riverbanks across the UK in spring, often smelt before it is seen. The broad leaves taste of mild garlic with a green, grassy note, and the white starry flowers and later the green seed pods are edible too. April is its peak.
Wild garlic.choose: Pick young, bright leaves before the plant flowers heavily, from clean areas away from paths and dogs, and crush one to check for a clear garlic smell.
Wild garlic.store: Keep unwashed in a bag in the fridge for three to four days, or blitz into a pesto or butter and freeze.
Wild garlic.prep: Wash well, then make pesto, wilt into risotto or soup, or stir into butter for steak and bread; add at the end as long cooking dulls it.
Wild garlic.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as the leaves can be confused with poisonous lily of the valley, lords and ladies, and young autumn crocus; only pick leaves that smell clearly of garlic, and check each one.

Three-cornered leek.about: Three-cornered leek is an invasive wild allium with white, bell-shaped flowers and stems that are triangular in cross-section, common in hedgebanks in the south and west of England. It tastes like a cross between spring onion and garlic, and the leaves, stems and flowers can all be eaten.
Three-cornered leek.choose: Pick fresh, green stems and leaves before the flowers go over, and check each stem for the triangular shape and onion smell.
Three-cornered leek.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge for up to four days.
Three-cornered leek.prep: Wash, then use like spring onions or chives, chopped into salads, omelettes and dressings or lightly fried; the flowers make a pretty garnish.
Three-cornered leek.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as young leaves can be mixed up with daffodils, snowdrops and bluebells; check for the three-sided stem and a strong onion smell on every one.

Nettles.about: Stinging nettles grow almost everywhere in the UK and the young spring tops are a free green with a flavour between spinach and cucumber, with plenty of iron. They are best in March and April before flowering, after which the leaves become coarse and gritty. Nettle soup is the classic use.
Nettles.choose: Pick only the top four to six leaves from young plants, wearing gloves, away from roadsides and sprayed field edges.
Nettles.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within two days.
Nettles.prep: Wash with gloves on, then blanch briefly to remove the sting; use in soup, risotto, gnocchi or anywhere you would use spinach.
Nettles.caution: Be sure of your ID, and only pick before the plant flowers, as older leaves contain gritty particles that can irritate the urinary tract.

Alexanders.about: Alexanders is a glossy, celery-like plant brought to Britain by the Romans and now common along coastal paths and hedges, especially in the south. The stems taste like a mix of celery and angelica with a slight myrrh note, and the black seeds were once used as a pepper substitute.
Alexanders.choose: Pick thick, young flower stalks before the yellow-green flowers open, and young shoots from near the base.
Alexanders.store: Keep the stems wrapped in damp paper in the fridge for up to five days.
Alexanders.prep: Peel the stringy outer skin from stems, then steam or boil and serve with butter like asparagus; the young leaves can go into soups and the dried seeds ground as a spice.
Alexanders.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as Alexanders belongs to the carrot family, which includes deadly hemlock and hemlock water dropwort; Alexanders has yellow-green flowers and glossy, three-part leaves.

Hop shoots.about: Hop shoots are the tender spring tips of the hop plant, picked from wild hedgerow hops and from the hop-growing areas of Kent and Herefordshire. They look and taste like thin, slightly bitter asparagus and have a very short season in April and May.
Hop shoots.choose: Pick the top 10 to 15 cm of young shoots that snap cleanly, avoiding tough or woody stems.
Hop shoots.store: Keep wrapped in damp paper in the fridge and use within two days.
Hop shoots.prep: Blanch for a minute or two and dress with butter or olive oil, or fold into an omelette or risotto.
Hop shoots.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as poisonous white bryony climbs in the same hedges; it has curly tendrils, while hops have hairy stems and no tendrils.

Dandelion leaves.about: Dandelion leaves are a common wild green with a bitter flavour similar to chicory or frisée. They are mildest in spring before the plant flowers, which is the time to pick them. In France a salad of dandelion leaves with hot bacon dressing is a classic.
Dandelion leaves.choose: Pick young, small leaves from the centre of the rosette, from areas away from roads, dogs and weedkiller.
Dandelion leaves.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge for two to three days.
Dandelion leaves.prep: Wash well and eat raw in salads with a warm, rich dressing to balance the bitterness, or wilt larger leaves in butter with garlic.
Dandelion leaves.caution: Be sure of your ID and only pick from ground you know has not been sprayed with weedkiller or fouled by dogs.

Wood sorrel.about: Wood sorrel is a small woodland plant with clover-like heart-shaped leaves in threes and delicate white flowers. Its taste is sharp and fresh, similar to green apple skin, and chefs often use it as a garnish. It grows in shady woods from spring into early autumn.
Wood sorrel.choose: Pick bright green leaves and flowers from clean, shady woodland, nipping off small sprigs rather than pulling up the plant.
Wood sorrel.store: Keep in a sealed box with damp kitchen paper in the fridge and use within a day or two.
Wood sorrel.prep: Rinse gently and use raw as a garnish for fish, salads and desserts, or chop into butter or dressings; cooking destroys its flavour.
Wood sorrel.caution: Wood sorrel contains oxalic acid, so eat it in small amounts, and be sure of your ID before picking.

Sea beet.about: Sea beet is the wild ancestor of beetroot, chard and spinach, growing on shingle beaches, sea walls and cliffs around the UK coast. The thick, glossy leaves taste like a meaty spinach with a hint of salt, and young spring leaves are the most tender, although it can be picked almost all year.
Sea beet.choose: Pick young, glossy, unblemished leaves from clean stretches of coast, avoiding plants near outfalls or dog walks.
Sea beet.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge for three to four days.
Sea beet.prep: Wash well and strip out tough stalks, then wilt in butter or steam briefly and use like spinach or chard.
Sea beet.caution: Be sure of your ID and only pick from clean coastline away from sewage outfalls.

Sea purslane.about: Sea purslane is a silvery grey-green shrub that grows in saltmarshes around the British coast, particularly in Norfolk and Essex. Its fleshy little leaves are crunchy and naturally salty, with a flavour a bit like a salty, juicy spinach. It is good with fish and lamb.
Sea purslane.choose: Pick young, plump leaves from the tips of shoots, from clean saltmarsh, and rinse off mud and grit.
Sea purslane.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge for up to a week.
Sea purslane.prep: Rinse thoroughly and eat raw in salads, or blanch briefly or toss in butter as a side for fish; go easy on any extra salt.
Sea purslane.caution: Be sure of your ID and avoid picking from marshes near sewage outfalls; take care with tides on saltmarsh.

Elderflower.about: Elderflower is the creamy-white, flat-topped blossom of the elder tree, which flowers in hedgerows across the UK in late May and June. The flowers have a sweet, musky, floral scent, and are best known for cordial and for flavouring gooseberries, which ripen at the same time.
Elderflower.choose: Pick fully open heads on a dry, sunny morning, from trees away from busy roads, and sniff them first: they should smell sweet, not musty.
Elderflower.store: Use within a few hours of picking, as the scent fades quickly; cordial keeps for weeks in the fridge or can be frozen.
Elderflower.prep: Shake off insects rather than washing, then steep the heads in syrup for cordial or in cream for desserts, or dip in batter and fry as fritters.
Elderflower.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as elder is a shrub, while cow parsley and poisonous hemlock have similar white flowers on ground plants; use the flowers only, as leaves, stems and bark are toxic.

Elderberries.about: Elderberries are the small, purple-black berries of the elder tree, hanging in heavy clusters in hedgerows in late summer and early autumn. They have a rich, tart, slightly earthy flavour, and are used for syrups, jellies and old English Pontack sauce, a spiced ketchup for game.
Elderberries.choose: Pick only heads where all the berries are fully dark and plump, avoiding any with green or red berries.
Elderberries.store: Keep in the fridge for a day or two, or freeze the heads, which also makes the berries easier to strip.
Elderberries.prep: Strip berries from the stalks with a fork, discard any stems and unripe fruit, then cook into syrup, jelly or crumbles, often with apples.
Elderberries.caution: Never eat elderberries raw, as raw berries, stems and leaves can cause sickness; always cook them thoroughly and remove all stalks.

Bilberries.about: Bilberries, called whinberries, whortleberries or blaeberries in different regions, are small wild cousins of the blueberry, found on moorland and heath in Wales, northern England and Scotland. Unlike cultivated blueberries, their flesh is purple right through, and they have a more intense, tart flavour.
Bilberries.choose: Pick plump, dark blue-black berries with a dusty bloom, from clean upland ground, and expect slow work as they grow low and singly.
Bilberries.store: Keep unwashed in a shallow box in the fridge for two to three days, or freeze on a tray.
Bilberries.prep: Rinse just before using and eat raw, bake into tarts and pies, or cook briefly with sugar for a compote.
Bilberries.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID before eating any wild berry, as several poisonous berries grow in similar places.

Wild strawberries.about: Wild strawberries are tiny red berries found along woodland edges, railway banks and hedgerows in summer. They have a much stronger, perfumed flavour than cultivated strawberries. The plants are also grown in gardens, where they are sold as alpine strawberries or fraises des bois.
Wild strawberries.choose: Pick only fully red, soft berries that come away easily, and look for the toothed three-part leaves and white flowers.
Wild strawberries.store: Eat on the day of picking; they bruise and spoil within hours.
Wild strawberries.prep: Avoid washing if possible, and eat raw with cream, over a tart or in a salad; their flavour is lost in cooking.
Wild strawberries.caution: Be sure of your ID before eating any wild berry.

Sloes.about: Sloes are the small, dusty blue-black fruit of the blackthorn, found in hedgerows across the UK in autumn. They are far too sour and astringent to eat raw, but steeped in gin with sugar they give sloe gin its colour and flavour, ready by Christmas if started in October.
Sloes.choose: Pick firm, dark fruit with a blue bloom, traditionally after the first frost, though freezing them at home does the same job.
Sloes.store: Keep in the fridge for a few days or freeze in bags until needed.
Sloes.prep: Freeze to split the skins, then steep in gin with sugar for two to three months, shaking occasionally; they also make jelly and sloe vodka.
Sloes.caution: Be sure of your ID, and do not crush the stones, which like other stone-fruit kernels contain compounds that release cyanide.

Rosehips.about: Rosehips are the red-orange seed pods left on wild roses, such as the dog rose, in autumn. They are tart and fruity and high in vitamin C, and during the Second World War children collected them so they could be made into rosehip syrup. They also make jelly.
Rosehips.choose: Pick firm, bright red hips that give slightly when pressed, avoiding shrivelled or blackened ones.
Rosehips.store: Keep in the fridge for up to a week, or freeze.
Rosehips.prep: Chop and simmer in water, then strain twice through a jelly bag to remove all the hairs before sweetening into syrup or jelly.
Rosehips.caution: The seeds are covered in irritant hairs, so always strain cooked rosehips through muslin or a jelly bag before eating.

Crab apples.about: Crab apples are small wild apples found in hedgerows and woods, and many ornamental varieties are grown in gardens. They are too sour to eat raw but are high in pectin, which makes them ideal for crab apple jelly, a classic accompaniment to lamb, pork and game.
Crab apples.choose: Pick firm, unblemished fruit as it ripens and starts to drop, and include some slightly underripe ones for extra pectin.
Crab apples.store: Keep in a cool place or the fridge for two to three weeks.
Crab apples.prep: Wash and chop roughly without peeling or coring, simmer until soft, then strain through a jelly bag and boil with sugar for jelly; add to other fruit to help it set.
Crab apples.caution: Be sure of your ID before eating any wild fruit, and discard the pips.

Sea buckthorn.about: Sea buckthorn is a thorny coastal shrub growing on dunes along the east coast of England, including Norfolk and Lincolnshire. Its bright orange berries are very sour, with a tropical flavour reminiscent of passion fruit and orange, and are rich in vitamin C.
Sea buckthorn.choose: Look for plump, bright orange berries, and wear gloves, since the branches are thorny and the berries burst easily.
Sea buckthorn.store: Freeze small sprigs whole, then shake off the berries once frozen; fresh berries keep only a day or two in the fridge.
Sea buckthorn.prep: Press or blitz and strain for juice, then sweeten into syrup, curd, jelly or sorbet, or use the sharp juice in dressings and sauces for fish.
Sea buckthorn.caution: Be sure of your ID before eating any wild berry.

Chestnut mushrooms.about: Chestnut mushrooms are a brown-capped strain of the common cultivated mushroom, with a firmer texture and deeper, nuttier flavour than white button mushrooms. They are grown in the UK all year, and when left to open fully they become portobellos.
Chestnut mushrooms.choose: Choose firm, dry mushrooms with tight caps and no slimy patches or dark wet spots.
Chestnut mushrooms.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge for up to a week, as plastic makes them sweat.
Chestnut mushrooms.prep: Wipe clean rather than washing, then fry hot in butter or oil without crowding the pan, or roast, add to stews, or use raw in salads.

Oyster mushrooms.about: Oyster mushrooms have fan-shaped caps in shades of grey, cream, yellow or pink and grow in clusters on wood. They have a soft, velvety texture and a mild, slightly sweet flavour. They are grown all year, often by small UK farms on straw or used coffee grounds, and also grow wild.
Oyster mushrooms.choose: Look for clusters with dry, springy caps and no yellow, wet or crumbling edges.
Oyster mushrooms.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge and use within three to four days.
Oyster mushrooms.prep: Tear rather than slice, then fry hot in oil until golden at the edges; they suit stir-fries, risottos and toast.

Shiitake.about: Shiitake are brown-capped mushrooms originally from East Asia, now grown all year in the UK on logs or blocks of sawdust. They have a meaty texture and a strong savoury flavour, and dried shiitake make an intense stock. The stems are tough and best kept for stock.
Shiitake.choose: Choose plump caps with curled-under edges and a dry, firm feel, avoiding any that are slimy or wrinkled.
Shiitake.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge for up to a week.
Shiitake.prep: Remove the tough stems, slice the caps and stir-fry, roast or add to broths and noodle soups.
Shiitake.caution: Cook shiitake thoroughly, as eating them raw or undercooked can cause an itchy skin rash in some people.

Morels.about: Morels are spring mushrooms with a hollow, honeycomb-pitted cap and an earthy, nutty, slightly smoky flavour. They are rare in the UK, occasionally found on disturbed ground, burnt sites and woodland edges, so most sold here are imported fresh or dried. Dried morels are very good, with concentrated flavour.
Morels.choose: Buy fresh morels that are dry and firm with no sliminess, or dried ones that look whole and smell earthy.
Morels.store: Keep fresh morels in a paper bag in the fridge for two to three days; dried ones keep for months in an airtight jar.
Morels.prep: Slice in half and rinse out grit and insects, or soak dried ones in warm water and use the strained liquid, then cook thoroughly in butter and cream.
Morels.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as the poisonous false morel has a brain-like, wrinkled cap that is not hollow, and always cook morels well, as they are toxic raw.

St George's mushrooms.about: St George's mushrooms are creamy white spring mushrooms named because they often appear around St George's Day on 23 April. They grow in rings in grassland, verges and woodland edges, and have a firm texture with a distinctive mealy smell and flavour. They are one of the few UK mushrooms that appear in spring.
St George's mushrooms.choose: Look for firm, white to cream caps with crowded white gills and a strong mealy smell; ask a supplier where they were found.
St George's mushrooms.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge and use within two to three days.
St George's mushrooms.prep: Brush clean, slice and fry in butter, then serve on toast, with eggs or in a creamy sauce with chicken.
St George's mushrooms.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as poisonous white fibrecaps and the livid pinkgill can look similar; a spore print should be white, never pink or brown.

Chicken of the woods.about: Chicken of the woods is a bright sulphur-yellow and orange bracket fungus growing in tiers on oak, willow, cherry and other trees. The young, tender edges have a meaty, slightly lemony flavour and a firm texture that is surprisingly like chicken, making it popular with vegetarians.
Chicken of the woods.choose: Choose young, soft, moist brackets that ooze slightly when squeezed, and trim off the tough, chalky older parts.
Chicken of the woods.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge for up to four days.
Chicken of the woods.prep: Slice and cook thoroughly, by frying, roasting or adding to stews and curries; it can be breaded and fried like chicken.
Chicken of the woods.caution: Always cook thoroughly, avoid brackets growing on yew, which may take up its toxins, and eat a small amount first as some people react badly.

Girolles (chanterelles).about: Girolles are golden-yellow mushrooms with a funnel-shaped cap and blunt ridges instead of true gills, found in mossy deciduous and conifer woods across the UK in late summer and autumn. They have a fruity, apricot-like smell and a delicate, peppery flavour.
Girolles (chanterelles).choose: Choose firm, dry, evenly coloured mushrooms with a fruity smell, avoiding any that are soggy or broken.
Girolles (chanterelles).store: Keep in a paper bag or lined basket in the fridge for up to five days.
Girolles (chanterelles).prep: Brush off soil and pine needles rather than washing, then fry in butter until golden and serve on toast, with eggs, pasta or chicken.
Girolles (chanterelles).caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as the false chanterelle looks similar but has thin, true gills and an orange colour, and some poisonous webcaps are also orange-brown.

Ceps (porcini).about: Ceps, also called penny buns or porcini, are fat-stemmed mushrooms with a brown, bun-like cap and sponge-like pores underneath instead of gills. They grow under oak, beech, birch and pine in late summer and autumn and have a rich, nutty, meaty flavour, which drying makes more intense.
Ceps (porcini).choose: Choose firm, heavy mushrooms with white or pale pores and no worm holes in the stem; older ones with yellow-green pores are softer and better for drying.
Ceps (porcini).store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge for two to three days, or slice and dry them for long keeping.
Ceps (porcini).prep: Brush and slice, then fry in butter or olive oil until golden, or use in risotto, pasta or with game; soak dried ceps and use the strained liquid.
Ceps (porcini).caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as the bitter bolete looks similar and ruins a dish, and some poisonous boletes have red pores or flesh that turns blue when cut.

Field mushrooms.about: Field mushrooms are the wild relatives of cultivated mushrooms, appearing in old grazing pasture after late summer rain. They have white caps and gills that start pink and turn chocolate brown, and their flavour is deeper and more mushroomy than shop-bought ones.
Field mushrooms.choose: Choose firm, fresh caps with pink to brown gills, and ask a supplier where they were picked.
Field mushrooms.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge and use within two to three days.
Field mushrooms.prep: Wipe clean, then fry in butter or grill whole and serve on toast, in a full breakfast, or in sauces with beef.
Field mushrooms.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as the deadly destroying angel has white gills, and the yellow stainer, which causes stomach upsets, turns bright yellow at the base of the stem when cut and smells of ink.

Hedgehog mushrooms.about: Hedgehog mushrooms have pale, buff-coloured caps with soft spines underneath instead of gills, and grow in woodland from late summer through autumn. They have a firm texture and a sweet, nutty flavour similar to girolles, and are among the easier wild mushrooms to recognise.
Hedgehog mushrooms.choose: Choose firm, clean mushrooms with intact spines and no wet or bruised patches.
Hedgehog mushrooms.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge for up to five days.
Hedgehog mushrooms.prep: Brush clean and scrape away the spines on older ones, then fry in butter, or use in risotto, omelettes and with game.
Hedgehog mushrooms.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID before eating any wild mushroom, and check that the underside has spines rather than gills or pores.

Giant puffball.about: The giant puffball is a large white fungus that can grow to the size of a football or larger, appearing in fields, parks and hedgerows from late summer. Young ones have firm, white flesh like a mild mushroom tofu and soak up flavour well. It is easy to recognise when large.
Giant puffball.choose: Choose one that feels firm and sounds slightly hollow, with pure white flesh when cut; discard any that are yellow, brown or spongy inside.
Giant puffball.store: Keep in the fridge wrapped loosely in paper and use within a few days; it does not freeze well.
Giant puffball.prep: Peel off the skin, cut into thick slices and fry in butter until golden, or coat in egg and breadcrumbs.
Giant puffball.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, and slice small specimens through to check the flesh is solid white, as the egg stage of a deadly amanita shows the outline of a mushroom inside.

Hen of the woods.about: Hen of the woods, also called maitake, is a large, frilly cluster of grey-brown caps that grows at the base of old oaks in autumn. It has a rich, earthy and slightly peppery flavour with a firm, meaty texture, and the crisp edges are excellent when roasted.
Hen of the woods.choose: Choose firm clusters with dry, grey-brown frills, avoiding any that are soggy or crumbly.
Hen of the woods.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge for up to five days.
Hen of the woods.prep: Tear into pieces, then roast or fry hard in oil until crisp at the edges, and season with butter, garlic and soy.
Hen of the woods.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as the giant polypore grows in similar places and is much tougher, and always cook it well.

Trompettes (horn of plenty).about: Trompettes, known in the UK as horn of plenty or black trumpets, are dark grey to black, trumpet-shaped mushrooms found in deciduous woodland leaf litter in autumn. They have an intense, earthy, smoky flavour and are easy to dry, which keeps the flavour well.
Trompettes (horn of plenty).choose: Choose dry, intact trumpets that smell earthy, avoiding any that are wet or broken up.
Trompettes (horn of plenty).store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge for up to five days, or dry for long keeping.
Trompettes (horn of plenty).prep: Split lengthways and wash well to remove grit, dry thoroughly, then fry briefly in butter with garlic, or add to risotto, eggs and sauces for game.
Trompettes (horn of plenty).caution: Be 100% sure of your ID before eating any wild mushroom.

Wood blewits.about: Wood blewits are late-season mushrooms with lilac-tinged caps and stems that become buff with age, growing in leaf litter, compost heaps and woodland from autumn into winter. They have a perfumed, slightly sweet aroma and a firm texture, and are traditionally cooked with onions or in stews.
Wood blewits.choose: Choose firm, clean caps with lilac gills and stem and a fragrant smell, avoiding any that are soggy.
Wood blewits.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge for up to five days.
Wood blewits.prep: Wipe clean and trim the stems, then cook thoroughly by frying in butter, or add to stews, sauces and omelettes.
Wood blewits.caution: Be 100% sure of your ID, as some poisonous webcaps also have purple tones; wood blewits give a pale pink spore print, never rusty brown, and must always be cooked.

English summer truffle.about: The English summer truffle grows underground among the roots of beech, oak and hazel trees on chalky soils in southern England, and is found by trained dogs. It has dark, knobbly skin and pale, marbled flesh, with a milder, nuttier aroma than the more expensive black Périgord truffle.
English summer truffle.choose: Choose firm truffles that feel heavy for their size and have a strong, earthy smell, avoiding any that are soft or spongy.
English summer truffle.store: Wrap in kitchen paper, changing it daily, in an airtight container in the fridge and use within a week.
English summer truffle.prep: Brush clean and shave thinly over hot pasta, risotto, eggs or potatoes, or infuse into butter; gentle heat brings out its aroma.

Mackerel.about: Mackerel is an oily fish with striped blue-green skin and rich, full-flavoured flesh. It arrives in large numbers off the south-west coast in summer, and handline-caught Cornish mackerel is one of the more sustainable choices in the UK. It is best eaten very fresh.
Mackerel.choose: Look for stiff, shiny fish with bright eyes, red gills and vivid markings; it should smell of the sea.
Mackerel.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within a day, as it spoils quickly.
Mackerel.prep: Grill, barbecue or pan-fry fillets skin side down until crisp, and serve with something sharp; it also cures well or can be hot-smoked.

Cornish sardines.about: Cornish sardines are pilchards caught by small ring-net boats off Cornwall, mainly from late summer into winter. They are small, oily and full of flavour, with tender flesh. The fishery is MSC certified, and pilchards have been a part of Cornish life for centuries.
Cornish sardines.choose: Look for bright, firm fish with shiny scales, clear eyes and a fresh sea smell; ask your fishmonger to scale and gut them.
Cornish sardines.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and cook on the day you buy them.
Cornish sardines.prep: Grill or barbecue whole, or fillet and pan-fry; serve with lemon, olive oil and herbs on toast or with salad.

Herring.about: Herring is a silver, oily fish with soft, rich flesh. It was once the mainstay of British fishing ports and remains the fish used for kippers, rollmops and bloaters. Clovelly in Devon holds a herring festival in November, when the local catch is at its best.
Herring.choose: Choose firm, bright fish with shiny scales, clear eyes and red gills; ask for them to be filleted and pin-boned.
Herring.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use within a day.
Herring.prep: Coat fillets in oatmeal and fry, grill with mustard, or pickle in sweetened vinegar for rollmops; watch for the many fine bones.

Sprats.about: Sprats are small, silvery oily fish related to herring, landed mainly from late autumn into winter. They have a rich, savoury flavour and are cheap, so they were traditionally a winter treat for Londoners, sold from the 9th of November, Lord Mayor's Day. They are eaten whole.
Sprats.choose: Choose bright, stiff fish with shiny silver skin and no strong fishy smell.
Sprats.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and cook on the day of buying.
Sprats.prep: Rinse and pat dry, dust in seasoned flour and fry in hot oil until crisp, then eat whole with lemon; they also grill and smoke well.

Cornish anchovies.about: Anchovies are small silver fish more associated with the Mediterranean, but shoals have appeared in large numbers off Cornwall in recent years, landed by the sardine fleet in autumn. Fresh anchovies are mild and delicate, quite unlike the salty tinned kind.
Cornish anchovies.choose: Look for small, very fresh fish with shiny skin, clear eyes and no softness; ask your fishmonger to confirm they were landed in Cornwall.
Cornish anchovies.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use on the day you buy them.
Cornish anchovies.prep: Remove the heads and guts, then either fry whole in flour or butterfly and marinate in vinegar, garlic and olive oil, Spanish boquerones style.

Sea bass (line-caught).about: Sea bass is a firm white fish with a clean, sweet flavour and crisp silver skin. Line-caught wild bass from British waters, at its best in late summer and early autumn, has a much better texture than farmed bass and is caught under strict size and catch limits to protect the stock.
Sea bass (line-caught).choose: Look for bright, clear eyes, red gills, firm flesh and a tag or label showing it was line-caught; ask your fishmonger where it was landed.
Sea bass (line-caught).store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within a day or two.
Sea bass (line-caught).prep: Score the skin and pan-fry skin side down until crisp, or bake whole with fennel and lemon; it is also excellent raw in ceviche when very fresh.

Pollock.about: Pollock is a white fish from the cod family, with soft, slightly flaky flesh and a mild, sweet flavour. Line-caught pollock from Cornwall and the south-west is a good-value, sustainable alternative to cod, and it works in any recipe that calls for white fish.
Pollock.choose: Look for firm, white to pale grey flesh that looks moist and smells fresh, with no browning at the edges.
Pollock.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use within a day or two.
Pollock.prep: Season and pan-fry, bake or roast; it is good in fish pies, fishcakes and battered fish, and firms up if lightly salted for 15 minutes first.

Hake.about: Hake is a long, silver-skinned white fish from the cod family, with soft, sweet, delicately flaky flesh. Cornish hake is MSC certified, but most of the UK catch has traditionally gone to Spain, where hake is the most popular fish. It cooks quickly and suits Spanish flavours.
Hake.choose: Look for firm, glossy white flesh and bright skin, with a fresh sea smell; avoid any that looks dull or watery.
Hake.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use within one to two days.
Hake.prep: Pan-fry skin side down and finish in the oven, or poach and serve with a green parsley sauce; handle gently as the flesh is soft.

Cod.about: Cod is the classic British white fish, with thick, pearly flakes and a clean, mild flavour. North Sea cod stocks have recovered in recent decades thanks to fishing limits, and line-caught or MSC-certified fish is the most sustainable choice. It is the traditional fish in fish and chips.
Cod.choose: Choose thick, translucent white fillets that are moist and firm, with no browning or strong smell; ask for MSC-certified or line-caught fish.
Cod.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use within one to two days.
Cod.prep: Roast, pan-fry or poach, salting the fillet for 15 minutes first to firm the flesh; it suits batter, fish pies and buttery sauces.

Haddock.about: Haddock is a cod relative with soft, sweet, slightly finer flakes and a distinct black line along its side. In Scotland and northern England it is the preferred fish for fish and chips, and it is the fish used for Arbroath smokies, finnan haddie and smoked haddock for kedgeree.
Haddock.choose: Look for firm, white, moist fillets with no sign of browning, and for smoked haddock choose undyed, pale golden fish.
Haddock.store: Keep fresh haddock in the coldest part of the fridge for one to two days; smoked haddock keeps a little longer.
Haddock.prep: Pan-fry, bake or batter fresh fillets; poach smoked haddock in milk for kedgeree, chowder or Cullen skink.

Coley.about: Coley, also called saithe, is a cod relative with grey-tinged flesh that turns white when cooked. It has a slightly stronger flavour and coarser texture than cod, and is cheap and widely available, making it a good choice for fish pies, fishcakes, curries and stews.
Coley.choose: Choose firm, moist fillets that smell fresh, and don't be put off by the grey colour.
Coley.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use within one to two days.
Coley.prep: Bake, pan-fry or cut into chunks for curries and stews, where its firm flakes hold up well.

Whiting.about: Whiting is a small white fish from the cod family, with soft, delicate flakes and a mild, sweet flavour. It is cheap and often overlooked, though it was once a common British supper fish, traditionally fried in breadcrumbs. It is landed around the UK coast through most of the year.
Whiting.choose: Choose bright, firm fish or fillets that look moist and smell fresh, avoiding any that look limp or dull.
Whiting.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use within a day, as the flesh is delicate.
Whiting.prep: Fry fillets in breadcrumbs or flour, or bake gently with butter and herbs; it is also good in fishcakes and goujons.

Ling.about: Ling is a long, slim fish from the cod family with firm, meaty white flesh and a mild flavour. It is often overlooked in the UK, though it is salted and dried in Scandinavia and Spain. It is a good, cheaper alternative to cod or monkfish, holding together well in stews.
Ling.choose: Look for firm, white, moist fillets with a fresh smell, from a fishmonger who can tell you where it was landed.
Ling.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use within one to two days.
Ling.prep: Roast, pan-fry or cut into chunks for stews and curries; it holds its shape well and can be wrapped in bacon or ham.

Plaice.about: Plaice is a flatfish with orange-spotted skin and soft, sweet, delicate white flesh. It is one of the most familiar British flatfish, landed in large numbers from the North Sea and the Channel, and is at its best in summer, after it has fed up following spawning.
Plaice.choose: Choose whole fish with bright orange spots, a slimy coating and firm flesh, or fillets that are moist and translucent.
Plaice.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use within a day or two.
Plaice.prep: Grill or pan-fry whole on the bone or as fillets in butter; it suits simple brown butter, capers, brown shrimp and herbs.

Lemon sole.about: Lemon sole is a flatfish with soft, sweet, delicate flesh and a mild flavour. It is not a true sole and is related to plaice and dab. It is landed around the British coast and is a good-value alternative to Dover sole, at its best from late summer through winter.
Lemon sole.choose: Choose bright, firm fish with slime on the skin and a clean sea smell, or moist, translucent fillets.
Lemon sole.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use within a day or two.
Lemon sole.prep: Grill or pan-fry whole or as fillets in butter, or bake gently with white wine; it cooks very quickly so watch it closely.

Dover sole.about: Dover sole is one of the finest British flatfish, with firm, meaty white flesh and a sweet, rich flavour. It is caught in the Channel and the North Sea and was historically brought into London via Dover. It improves if eaten a day or two after catching, and the classic dish is sole meunière.
Dover sole.choose: Choose firm fish with a shiny, bright skin and a fresh sea smell, and ask your fishmonger to skin it.
Dover sole.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within two to three days.
Dover sole.prep: Grill or pan-fry whole on the bone in butter, then finish with lemon and parsley; the flesh lifts easily from the bone once cooked.

Megrim (Cornish sole).about: Megrim is a thin, sandy-coloured flatfish with soft, sweet flesh, landed mainly in Cornwall. Most of the catch was traditionally exported to Spain, so it was rebranded as Cornish sole to make it more popular in the UK. It is a cheap and sustainable alternative to lemon or Dover sole.
Megrim (Cornish sole).choose: Choose bright, firm fish with clear eyes and a fresh smell, or moist, translucent fillets.
Megrim (Cornish sole).store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge and use within a day or two.
Megrim (Cornish sole).prep: Grill or pan-fry whole or as fillets in butter, as the flesh is fine and cooks quickly; it suits brown butter, capers and herbs.

Dab.about: A small, sweet-fleshed flatfish landed all round the British coast and often overlooked in favour of plaice. Its flesh is delicate and slightly sweet, and because it is cheap and plentiful it is one of the best-value fish on the slab. It eats best from late summer through winter, before spawning in spring.
Dab.choose: Look for bright, slimy skin, clear eyes and a firm body that springs back when pressed, and ask the fishmonger to trim and gut them.
Dab.store: Keep in the coldest part of the fridge, covered, and cook within a day or two.
Dab.prep: Cook whole on the bone: dust in seasoned flour and pan-fry in butter for a few minutes a side, or grill and finish with a squeeze of lemon.

Turbot.about: The most prized of British flatfish, with thick, firm white flesh and a rich, clean flavour that comes from its high gelatin content. Most of the wild catch comes from the south-west and the North Sea. It is in good condition from late summer into early spring, and a whole one roasted on the bone is a proper occasion fish.
Turbot.choose: Choose fish with bright, unblemished skin, clear eyes and a fresh sea smell; the dark top side should be glossy and the flesh firm.
Turbot.store: Store well wrapped in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within two days.
Turbot.prep: Roast or grill whole or in thick bone-in steaks to keep the flesh moist, and serve with a butter sauce; the bones and head make excellent stock.

Brill.about: A large flatfish closely related to turbot, with slightly softer, sweeter flesh and smooth, scale-covered skin. It costs noticeably less than turbot and can be cooked in all the same ways. Brill is in good condition from summer through winter and is landed mainly off the south and west coasts.
Brill.choose: Look for glossy skin, bright eyes and firm flesh with a clean sea smell; fillets should look translucent with no gaping.
Brill.store: Keep covered in the coldest part of the fridge and use within two days.
Brill.prep: Roast whole or on the bone, or pan-fry fillets skin-side down in butter; it takes well to cider, mussels and creamy sauces.

John Dory.about: An odd-looking, flat-sided fish with a dark spot on each flank, said in legend to be the thumbprint of St Peter. Its firm, white, sweet flesh is among the best in British waters, and Cornish day boats land it through summer and autumn. Yield is low, so expect to pay for the head and frame.
John Dory.choose: Choose fish with bright, firm bodies, intact spines and a clear, distinct spot; ask the fishmonger to fillet it and keep the frame for stock.
John Dory.store: Store covered in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within a day or two.
John Dory.prep: Pan-fry the fillets skin-side down in butter or olive oil for a few minutes, or roast whole; serve simply with lemon or a light butter sauce.

Monkfish.about: A deep-water fish with a huge head and a firm, meaty tail that is the part usually sold. The flesh is sweet and dense, holds together well and has only one central bone. It is landed year round in the south-west, but quality is good from summer through winter.
Monkfish.choose: Choose tails with moist, white flesh and a clean smell, and ask the fishmonger to remove the grey membrane for you.
Monkfish.store: Keep wrapped in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within two days.
Monkfish.prep: Strip off any remaining membrane, then roast on the bone, wrap in ham and roast, or cut into chunks for curries, kebabs and stews.

Gurnard.about: A bony, armoured-looking fish with a big head and red or grey skin, once used mainly as pot bait. Its firm white flesh has a good, sweet flavour, and it is a sustainable, cheap alternative to more fashionable white fish. It is at its best in late summer and autumn, landed largely off Cornwall.
Gurnard.choose: Look for bright skin, clear eyes and firm flesh, and buy it filleted unless you want the head and bones for a fish soup.
Gurnard.store: Store covered in the fridge and cook within a day or two.
Gurnard.prep: Pan-fry or roast fillets, or use whole fish in stews and soups such as bouillabaisse; watch for pin bones.

Red mullet.about: A small, rosy-pink fish with firm, sweet flesh and a distinctive, almost shellfish-like flavour; the liver is prized and traditionally left in. It is at its best in high summer, when Cornish boats land it in good numbers. It pairs naturally with Mediterranean summer vegetables.
Red mullet.choose: Choose bright red-pink fish with firm bodies, clear eyes and scales intact; the colour fades as it ages.
Red mullet.store: Keep covered in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within a day.
Red mullet.prep: Scale carefully, then grill or barbecue whole, or pan-fry fillets skin-side down until crisp; pin-bone fillets before cooking.

Grey mullet.about: A silvery, thick-lipped fish common in British estuaries and harbours, with firm, meaty flesh similar to sea bass. Fish from clean, open water taste mild and sweet, while those from muddy estuaries can taste earthy. It is underused and cheap, and good from summer into winter.
Grey mullet.choose: Buy from a fishmonger who knows where it was caught, choosing firm, bright fish from clean coastal water.
Grey mullet.store: Store covered in the fridge and cook within a day or two.
Grey mullet.prep: Scale well, then grill, roast whole or pan-fry fillets with crisp skin; strong flavours such as ginger, chilli and herbs suit it.

Black bream.about: A deep-bodied, silver-grey sea bream with firm, white, sweet flesh, popular with anglers along the south coast. Large numbers come inshore off Sussex and Dorset in spring to breed, and the fishery is managed to protect them while they nest. It makes an excellent, cheaper alternative to sea bass.
Black bream.choose: Look for bright, firm fish with clear eyes and red gills, and ask for it to be scaled and gutted.
Black bream.store: Store covered in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within two days.
Black bream.prep: Slash and grill or barbecue whole, or pan-fry fillets skin-side down; it also works raw as ceviche if very fresh.

Skate & ray.about: Cartilaginous flat fish sold as wings, with sweet, ribbon-like flesh that slides cleanly off soft cartilage instead of bones. Thornback, blonde and cuckoo ray are the species most often sold in the UK, and some stocks are better managed than others. Skate wing with black butter and capers is a bistro classic.
Skate & ray.choose: Ask which species it is and where it was caught, and choose wings that smell clean and sweet; any whiff of ammonia means it is past its best.
Skate & ray.store: Keep wrapped in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within a day or two.
Skate & ray.prep: Pan-fry or poach whole wings, then lift the flesh from the cartilage; serve with brown butter, capers and parsley.

Wild brown trout.about: Britain's native river and loch trout, with golden, spotted skin and delicate, sweet flesh that tastes of the water it lived in. It is rarely sold commercially, so most comes from anglers, who fish for it in the chalk streams of southern England and Scottish lochs. The season runs from spring to early autumn.
Wild brown trout.choose: Wild brown trout is seldom sold, so get it from an angler; look for bright, slimy skin, clear eyes and a fresh, clean smell.
Wild brown trout.store: Gut promptly and keep cold in the fridge, cooking within a day or two.
Wild brown trout.prep: Cook whole: pan-fry in butter, grill or bake in foil with herbs; it needs little more than lemon and almonds.

Sea trout.about: A brown trout that has gone to sea and returns to British rivers to spawn, known as sewin in Wales. Its pink flesh is more delicate and finer-textured than salmon, with a cleaner flavour. Supplies are limited and mostly from licensed net fisheries and anglers, with the best fish in late spring and early summer.
Sea trout.choose: Look for bright silver fish with firm flesh and clear eyes, and ask the fishmonger where and how it was caught.
Sea trout.store: Store covered in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within two days.
Sea trout.prep: Poach whole, bake in foil, or pan-fry fillets skin-side down; serve with hollandaise or a herb butter.

Rainbow trout.about: A farmed freshwater trout available all year, with mild, sweet flesh that is either white or pink depending on its feed. Much of the UK supply comes from farms in Hampshire, Yorkshire and Scotland. It is cheap and quick to cook, and smoked rainbow trout is a good alternative to smoked salmon.
Rainbow trout.choose: Choose bright, firm fish with clear eyes and a fresh smell, from a farm with good welfare standards if you can.
Rainbow trout.store: Keep covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Rainbow trout.prep: Pan-fry or grill whole or as fillets, or bake in foil with herbs; it also smokes and cures well.

Pike.about: A large predatory freshwater fish with firm, white, slightly sweet flesh, widely eaten in France and central Europe but rarely in Britain. It is caught by coarse anglers in rivers and lakes from summer through winter. Its many Y-shaped bones make it fiddly, which is why it is classically turned into quenelles.
Pike.choose: Pike is rarely sold, so ask an angler or specialist fishmonger; choose fish with clean-smelling, firm flesh and slimy skin.
Pike.store: Gut promptly, keep covered in the fridge and cook within a day or two.
Pike.prep: Fillet and remove the Y-bones, then pan-fry or bake, or blend the flesh into quenelles or fishcakes; serve with a rich sauce.

Mussels.about: Blue mussels are rope-grown in Shetland and the west of Scotland and gathered from beds in Devon, Cornwall and Wales. They are sweet, briny and among the cheapest, most sustainable seafood you can buy. They are at their plumpest in the colder months and thinner after spawning in late spring and summer.
Mussels.choose: Choose mussels with tightly closed or closing shells that smell of the sea, and avoid any that are cracked or very heavy with sand.
Mussels.store: Keep in a bowl in the fridge covered with a damp cloth, never in water or a sealed bag, and cook within a day or two.
Mussels.prep: Rinse, pull off the beards, then steam with wine or cider, shallots and herbs for a few minutes until they open.
Mussels.caution: Discard any that are open and don't close when tapped before cooking, and any that stay shut after cooking.

Native oysters.about: The flat European oyster, native to British waters and far less common than the farmed rock oyster. They have a rich, mineral, almost metallic flavour and are usually eaten raw. Fisheries such as the Fal, still dredged under sail and oar, and those around Colchester and Whitstable are only open in the months with an 'r'.
Native oysters.choose: Buy live from a reputable fishmonger, choosing oysters that feel heavy and are tightly closed.
Native oysters.store: Store cup-side down in the fridge under a damp cloth and eat within two or three days.
Native oysters.prep: Shuck with a proper oyster knife and eat raw with lemon or shallot vinegar; natives are rarely cooked.
Native oysters.caution: Eat raw oysters only from a trusted supplier, discard any that are open or don't smell fresh, and avoid raw oysters if pregnant or vulnerable.

Rock oysters.about: Pacific rock oysters are farmed around the British coast and available all year, though they are plumpest and best from autumn through spring. They are deeper-cupped and creamier than natives, with a fresh, briny flavour. Farms in Cornwall, Essex, Kent and the west of Scotland all produce good ones.
Rock oysters.choose: Choose oysters that are tightly closed, feel heavy for their size and smell clean and of the sea.
Rock oysters.store: Store cup-side down in the fridge under a damp cloth and eat within three or four days.
Rock oysters.prep: Eat raw with lemon or shallot vinegar, or grill on the half shell with butter and breadcrumbs.
Rock oysters.caution: Eat raw oysters only from a trusted supplier, discard any that are open or don't smell fresh, and avoid raw oysters if pregnant or vulnerable.

King scallops (hand-dived).about: Large, sweet scallops gathered by divers, which avoids the seabed damage caused by dredging. The flesh is tender and sugary, with a bright orange roe that many cooks prize. Hand-dived scallops come from Scotland, Lyme Bay and the south-west, and are best through autumn and winter before spawning.
King scallops (hand-dived).choose: Buy live in the shell or freshly shucked, choosing plump, creamy-white, dry-looking meat with a sweet smell and no milky liquid.
King scallops (hand-dived).store: Keep shucked scallops covered in the coldest part of the fridge and use within a day.
King scallops (hand-dived).prep: Pat dry and sear in a very hot pan for about a minute each side, leaving the centre just translucent; the shells also work as baking dishes.

Queen scallops.about: Small scallops, about the size of a thumbnail, fished around the Isle of Man where they are called queenies. They are sweet and tender and cook in seconds. The Isle of Man fishery is certified as sustainable and they are best in summer and autumn.
Queen scallops.choose: Choose plump, ivory-coloured meat that smells sweet and fresh, or live ones in the shell that close when tapped.
Queen scallops.store: Keep covered in the coldest part of the fridge and use within a day.
Queen scallops.prep: Flash-fry in butter with garlic, or grill in the half shell topped with garlic butter and breadcrumbs.

Brown crab.about: The heavy-shelled crab of British waters, prized for its sweet white claw meat and rich, savoury brown body meat. Cromer crab from the Norfolk coast is the best-known name, and Devon and Cornwall land large quantities. The meat is fullest in summer and early autumn.
Brown crab.choose: Choose crabs that feel heavy for their size, and favour cock crabs for more white meat; dressed crab should smell sweet and fresh.
Brown crab.store: Keep cooked crab or picked meat covered in the fridge and eat within two days.
Brown crab.prep: Buy ready cooked or boil live crab in well-salted water for about 15 minutes per kilo, then pick the white and brown meat for sandwiches, salads or pasta.

Spider crab.about: A long-legged, spiny crab that arrives off the coasts of Devon and Cornwall in spring. Its sweet, delicate meat is more highly regarded in Spain and France, where most of the British catch is exported. Buying it locally supports south-west fishermen and it is often cheaper than brown crab.
Spider crab.choose: Choose crabs that feel heavy for their size and have all their legs; buy cooked or live from a good fishmonger.
Spider crab.store: Keep cooked crab covered in the fridge and eat within two days.
Spider crab.prep: Boil live crab in salted water for about 15 minutes, then pick the meat from the legs and body; it suits pasta, salads and toast.

Lobster.about: The European blue-black lobster, caught in pots around the British and Irish coast, turns red when cooked. Its firm, sweet meat is one of the great luxuries of the summer table. Cornwall, Northumberland and the Scottish coast land most of the UK catch, with prices lowest at the height of summer.
Lobster.choose: Choose a lively, heavy lobster with both claws, or ask the fishmonger to cook one for you.
Lobster.store: Keep live lobster in the fridge under a damp cloth and cook the same day; cooked lobster keeps up to two days in the fridge.
Lobster.prep: Boil whole in well-salted water, or split and grill with butter; serve with chips, a green salad or mayonnaise.

Langoustines.about: Also called Dublin Bay prawns or Norway lobster, these slim, pale orange shellfish come mostly from Scottish waters. Their sweet, delicate tail meat is closer to lobster than to prawns. Creel-caught langoustines from the west coast of Scotland are the best quality, as they are landed in better condition.
Langoustines.choose: Buy live or very fresh, choosing creel-caught ones with intact shells and no blackening at the head.
Langoustines.store: Cook live langoustines on the day you buy them; cooked ones keep a day or two in the fridge.
Langoustines.prep: Boil or steam for two or three minutes, or split and grill with garlic butter; peel and eat with mayonnaise.

Clams.about: The UK lands and farms several species, including palourde and Manila clams, mainly from the south coast and Poole Harbour. They are sweet, briny and quick to cook, and best in the colder months. Spaghetti alle vongole is the obvious and best use for them.
Clams.choose: Buy live clams that are tightly closed or close when tapped, with no broken shells and a fresh sea smell.
Clams.store: Keep in a bowl in the fridge covered with a damp cloth and cook within a day or two.
Clams.prep: Soak in salted water to purge any sand, then steam open in a covered pan with wine and garlic.
Clams.caution: Discard any that are open and don't close when tapped before cooking, and any that stay shut after cooking.

Cockles.about: Small, ribbed bivalves raked from sandbanks around the UK, with famous beds at Penclawdd on the Gower and Stiffkey in Norfolk. They are sweet, salty and chewy, and traditionally eaten from a pot with vinegar and pepper at the seaside. In south Wales they are fried with laverbread and bacon for breakfast.
Cockles.choose: Buy live in the shell from a trusted fishmonger, choosing cockles that are closed or close when tapped.
Cockles.store: Keep in a bowl in the fridge under a damp cloth and cook within a day.
Cockles.prep: Soak in several changes of salted water to remove sand, then steam open; eat with vinegar or add to pasta, rice and chowder.
Cockles.caution: Discard any that are open and don't close when tapped before cooking, and any that stay shut after cooking.

Razor clams.about: Long, thin clams with a sweet, meaty flavour, dug or hand-dived from sandy beaches around Scotland and Wales. They cook in a minute or two and have a firmer bite than ordinary clams. They look dramatic on the plate and are good value compared with scallops.
Razor clams.choose: Buy live, choosing razors that retract or move when touched and have unbroken shells.
Razor clams.store: Keep in the fridge under a damp cloth and cook the same day or the next.
Razor clams.prep: Rinse, then steam or grill for a minute or two until they open; remove the dark gut, slice the meat and dress with garlic, chilli and herbs.
Razor clams.caution: Discard any that are open and don't close when tapped before cooking, and any that stay shut after cooking.

Winkles.about: Small sea snails gathered from rocks around the British coast, traditionally sold cooked in paper bags at seaside stalls and East London shellfish stalls. They have a chewy texture and a sweet, salty, seaweedy taste. They are cheap and plentiful through the colder months.
Winkles.choose: Buy from a trusted fishmonger, choosing live winkles that retract into the shell when touched, or freshly cooked ones.
Winkles.store: Keep live winkles in the fridge under a damp cloth and cook within a day; eat cooked ones within two days.
Winkles.prep: Rinse well and boil in salted water for about five minutes, then winkle out the meat with a pin after removing the little hard cap.
Winkles.caution: Buy only from a reputable supplier and discard any that don't retract when touched before cooking.

Brown shrimp.about: Tiny, sweet grey-brown shrimps caught in shallow waters, most famously in Morecambe Bay and off the Lincolnshire and Norfolk coasts. They are cooked on the boat and are fiddly to peel but full of flavour. Potted in spiced butter, they are a British classic.
Brown shrimp.choose: Buy them cooked, peeled or unpeeled, and look for a sweet smell and a firm, moist texture.
Brown shrimp.store: Keep in the fridge and eat within two days; potted shrimps keep a little longer under their butter seal.
Brown shrimp.prep: Eat on toast, in omelettes or with fish, or pot them in butter spiced with mace and cayenne.

Squid.about: Squid come close to the south coast of England in autumn, when Sussex, Devon and Cornwall boats land them, and jig-caught local squid is a world away from frozen imports. The flesh is sweet and tender if cooked very quickly or very slowly. It is good value and suits big flavours.
Squid.choose: Choose squid with glossy, firm bodies, intact skin and a clean sea smell; the bigger the eyes and brighter the skin, the fresher it is.
Squid.store: Keep covered in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within a day or two, or clean and freeze.
Squid.prep: Clean, score and cook fast on a very hot griddle or deep-fry, or braise slowly with tomatoes and wine.

Cuttlefish.about: A relative of squid that comes into the English Channel in spring to spawn, landed mainly in Sussex, Dorset and Devon. The flesh is thicker and sweeter than squid, and the ink is used to colour rice and pasta. Most of the catch is exported to Spain and Italy, so it can be cheap when you find it.
Cuttlefish.choose: Choose shiny, firm cuttlefish with a clean sea smell, and ask the fishmonger to clean it and keep the ink sac if you want it.
Cuttlefish.store: Keep covered in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within a day or two.
Cuttlefish.prep: Grill or fry quickly after scoring, or stew slowly with tomato and wine until tender; use the ink for black risotto.

New-season lamb.about: Lamb born in late winter and spring and eaten from early summer, with pale, tender meat and a mild, sweet flavour. Breed and grazing matter: Welsh lamb, Romney Marsh salt marsh lamb and Herdwick from the Lake District all taste distinctive. It is at its best and best value from late summer into autumn.
New-season lamb.choose: Look for pale pink to light red meat with firm, creamy-white fat, and ask the butcher about the breed and where it was raised.
New-season lamb.store: Store covered in the fridge for up to three days, or freeze.
New-season lamb.prep: Roast legs and shoulders, grill chops and cutlets pink, or slow-cook shoulder until it falls apart.

Hogget.about: Sheep between one and two years old, with deeper colour, fuller flavour and more fat than young lamb. It fills the gap in late winter and spring before new-season lamb arrives. Hogget from hill breeds is especially good, and many butchers think it has the best balance of tenderness and flavour.
Hogget.choose: Look for darker meat than lamb with good creamy fat cover, and buy from a butcher who hangs it for at least a week.
Hogget.store: Store covered in the fridge for up to three days, or freeze.
Hogget.prep: Slow-roast or braise shoulder and leg, or roast rack and loin pink; it takes strong herbs and spices well.

Mutton.about: Meat from sheep over two years old, with a deep colour and strong, rich flavour that was standard on British tables until the mid-20th century. It needs long, slow cooking and is good value. Mutton is at its best in autumn and winter, after the sheep have fattened on summer grazing.
Mutton.choose: Choose meat that is deep red with firm, white fat, from a butcher who has hung it for at least two weeks.
Mutton.store: Store covered in the fridge for up to three days, or freeze.
Mutton.prep: Braise, stew or slow-roast for several hours; it is ideal for curries, hotpots and mutton with caper sauce.

Beef.about: British beef is available all year, with native breeds such as Aberdeen Angus, Hereford and Dexter known for good marbling and flavour. Grass-fed beef from good pasture and properly dry-aged meat taste markedly better than standard supermarket cuts. Slow-cooking cuts come into their own in autumn and winter.
Beef.choose: Choose meat that is deep red with creamy-white fat and good marbling, and ask the butcher how long it has been dry-aged.
Beef.store: Store covered on the bottom shelf of the fridge: steaks and joints for up to three days, mince for one or two.
Beef.prep: Roast rib or sirloin, grill or fry steaks, and braise shin, cheek and brisket slowly in stock or ale.

Pork.about: British pork is produced all year, and outdoor-bred or free-range pigs from traditional breeds such as Gloucester Old Spot, Tamworth and Berkshire give richer, more flavourful meat. Good crackling depends on dry, well-scored skin. Autumn apples and pork are a classic British pairing.
Pork.choose: Look for pale pink meat with firm, white fat and dry skin, and choose outdoor-reared pork from a named farm where possible.
Pork.store: Store uncovered or loosely covered on the bottom shelf of the fridge for up to three days.
Pork.prep: Roast belly or shoulder slowly for crackling, grill chops, or braise cheeks and hocks; cook through until the juices run clear.

Free-range chicken.about: Free-range chickens have outdoor access and are usually grown more slowly than intensively reared birds, giving firmer meat and more flavour. Breeds such as Label Anglais and Cotswold White are raised for flavour. They are available all year and a whole bird is the most economical way to buy.
Free-range chicken.choose: Choose a plump bird with unbroken, creamy skin and a clean smell, from a butcher or farm that tells you how it was reared.
Free-range chicken.store: Store covered on the bottom shelf of the fridge and use within two days of buying, or by the use-by date.
Free-range chicken.prep: Roast whole, joint and braise, or poach; use the carcass for stock and cook through until the juices run clear.

Duck.about: Farmed duck is available all year, with Gressingham and Aylesbury the best-known British types. The meat is rich and dark with a thick layer of fat that renders into good roasting fat. Its richness suits sharp fruit such as cherries in summer and oranges in winter.
Duck.choose: Choose a plump bird or breasts with dry, creamy skin and a thick fat layer, and avoid any with a sticky surface.
Duck.store: Store uncovered on the bottom shelf of the fridge so the skin dries, and use within two days.
Duck.prep: Score the breast skin and render it slowly skin-side down before finishing pink; roast whole birds and slow-cook legs.

Guinea fowl.about: A bird originally from Africa, farmed in Britain and France, with flesh somewhere between chicken and pheasant: slightly gamey and darker than chicken. It is available all year and makes a good change from chicken for a Sunday roast. The meat is lean, so it benefits from bacon or butter.
Guinea fowl.choose: Choose a plump, firm bird with clean skin, and ask the butcher whether it is free-range.
Guinea fowl.store: Store covered on the bottom shelf of the fridge and use within two days.
Guinea fowl.prep: Roast with butter or bacon over the breast, or joint and braise with wine and mushrooms; cook through until the juices run clear.

Goose.about: A rich, dark-fleshed bird with plenty of fat, traditionally eaten at Michaelmas (29 September) and at Christmas. Free-range geese are reared on grass through the summer and are ready from autumn. One bird feeds fewer people than its size suggests, but the rendered fat is excellent for roast potatoes.
Goose.choose: Order a free-range goose from a farm or butcher well ahead of Christmas, choosing a plump, dry-skinned bird.
Goose.store: Store loosely covered on the bottom shelf of the fridge and cook within three days of buying.
Goose.prep: Prick the skin and roast on a rack, pouring off the fat as it collects; save it for roasting potatoes.

Free-range turkey.about: Free-range turkey from slow-growing breeds such as Norfolk Black and Bronze has firmer meat and much more flavour than intensively reared birds. Most are reared for Christmas, with Norfolk the traditional heartland. A properly hung bird cooks faster and stays moister than many cooks expect.
Free-range turkey.choose: Order early from a farm or butcher, ask whether it has been dry-plucked and hung, and buy for the number of people you are feeding.
Free-range turkey.store: Store on the bottom shelf of the fridge, loosely covered, and cook by the use-by date.
Free-range turkey.prep: Roast with butter under the skin and bacon over the breast, and rest it well before carving; cook through until the juices run clear.

Grouse.about: Red grouse is a wild bird from the moors of Scotland and northern England, and the season opens on the Glorious Twelfth of August. It has dark, strongly flavoured meat with a heathery taste that comes from its diet. Young birds early in the season are the most tender.
Grouse.choose: Buy from a game dealer or butcher, ask whether it is a young bird, and look for an undamaged breast.
Grouse.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two or three days.
Grouse.prep: Roast young birds hot and fast for about 15 minutes, leaving them pink, and serve on toast with bread sauce; braise older birds.
Grouse.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.

Snipe.about: A small wild wader, shot from August to January, with rich, dark meat and a strong, gamey flavour. Each bird is about one serving for a starter. Like woodcock, it is traditionally cooked with its innards (the trail) left in and served on toast.
Snipe.choose: Snipe is rarely sold, so ask a game dealer; look for plump, well-feathered birds with intact breasts.
Snipe.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Snipe.prep: Roast hot for about ten minutes, then serve on fried bread or toast spread with the cooked innards.
Snipe.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.

Partridge.about: The UK has two kinds: the native grey partridge and the more common red-legged (French) partridge. The meat is pale, tender and mildly gamey, which makes it a good introduction to game. The season opens on 1 September and partridge is at its best in autumn.
Partridge.choose: Buy oven-ready from a game dealer or butcher, choosing plump birds with unbroken skin.
Partridge.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two or three days.
Partridge.prep: Roast hot for about 20 minutes, or pot-roast with cabbage and bacon; one bird serves one.
Partridge.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.

Pheasant.about: The most common game bird in Britain, shot from 1 October to 1 February. Hen birds are smaller and more tender, while cocks are larger. The meat is lean and mildly gamey, and plentiful supply makes it cheap at butchers and game dealers through the winter.
Pheasant.choose: Buy a brace (cock and hen) or oven-ready birds from a game dealer, choosing plump birds with little shot damage.
Pheasant.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two or three days.
Pheasant.prep: Roast with bacon over the breast, or pot-roast and braise to keep the lean meat moist; legs are good slow-cooked.
Pheasant.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.

Woodcock.about: A small, secretive woodland wader that is among the most prized of British game birds. Its dark meat is rich and deeply flavoured, and it is traditionally roasted with the guts in and served on toast. The shooting season in England runs from October to January.
Woodcock.choose: Woodcock is rarely sold, so ask a game dealer; look for plump, intact birds.
Woodcock.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Woodcock.prep: Roast hot for about 12 to 15 minutes, then serve on fried bread spread with the cooked innards.
Woodcock.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.

Mallard.about: The largest and most common wild duck in Britain, shot from September to January. It has darker, leaner and gamier meat than farmed duck, with a good depth of flavour. A single mallard serves two, and birds that have fed inland on grain are usually better eating than those from the coast.
Mallard.choose: Buy from a game dealer or butcher, choosing plump birds with intact breasts.
Mallard.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two or three days.
Mallard.prep: Roast whole for about 30 minutes and serve pink, or pan-fry breasts and slow-cook the legs.
Mallard.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.

Teal.about: The smallest British wild duck, with fine, dark meat that is sweeter and more delicate than mallard. One bird serves one person. The season runs from September to January, and teal is one of the best-flavoured of the wildfowl.
Teal.choose: Teal is rarely sold, so ask a game dealer; look for plump, well-feathered birds.
Teal.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Teal.prep: Roast hot for about 15 minutes and serve pink, or pan-fry the breasts quickly.
Teal.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.

Wild venison.about: Meat from wild red, roe, fallow and muntjac deer, culled to manage numbers across Britain. It is very lean, dark and mildly gamey, and each species has its own open season. It is one of the healthiest and most sustainable meats available.
Wild venison.choose: Ask the butcher which species it is; roe and fallow are milder and more tender, while red deer is more strongly flavoured.
Wild venison.store: Store covered in the fridge for up to three days, or freeze.
Wild venison.prep: Sear loins and haunch steaks quickly and serve pink, or slow-cook shoulder and shin in stews and pies.
Wild venison.caution: Wild venison may contain lead fragments from the bullet, so buy from a trusted dealer and trim around the wound channel.

Hare.about: Brown hare has dark, rich and strongly flavoured meat, quite different from rabbit. Jugged hare, cooked with red wine and thickened with the blood, is the classic British dish. Hare cannot be sold from March to July, so it is an autumn and winter meat.
Hare.choose: Buy from a game dealer, preferably a young hare (leveret), already skinned and jointed.
Hare.store: Store covered in the fridge and cook within two or three days.
Hare.prep: Slow-cook legs in red wine for stews and ragù, and cook the saddle fillets quickly so they stay pink.
Hare.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.

Wild rabbit.about: Wild rabbit is cheap and available all year in Britain, with no closed season. It is leaner and has more flavour than farmed rabbit, with sweet, pale meat. It is at its best from autumn to spring, and a single rabbit feeds two.
Wild rabbit.choose: Buy from a game dealer or butcher, ideally skinned and jointed, and look for young rabbits with pale, moist meat.
Wild rabbit.store: Store covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Wild rabbit.prep: Braise or slow-cook with mustard, cider or wine to stop the lean meat drying out; the saddle can be roasted quickly.
Wild rabbit.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.

Wood pigeon.about: A wild bird shot all year as a crop pest, with dark, lean meat that is milder than most game. The breasts are the main part eaten and are cheap and quick to cook. It is plumpest from late spring to autumn after feeding on crops.
Wood pigeon.choose: Buy whole birds or breasts from a game dealer, choosing plump, deep red breasts with no strong smell.
Wood pigeon.store: Store covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Wood pigeon.prep: Sear breasts in a hot pan for two minutes a side and serve pink, or slow-cook whole birds in a casserole.
Wood pigeon.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.

Kentish cobnuts.about: A cultivated hazelnut grown in Kent orchards since Victorian times, most commonly the Kentish Cob variety. They are sold fresh, starting with green husks and white, juicy kernels in August and turning brown and sweeter by autumn. Fresh cobnuts have a milky, slightly sweet crunch quite unlike dried hazelnuts.
Kentish cobnuts.choose: Choose nuts with fresh, unblemished husks and heavy, full shells.
Kentish cobnuts.store: Store in a paper bag in the fridge for up to two weeks.
Kentish cobnuts.prep: Crack and eat raw, or toast them lightly; they suit salads, pesto, crumbles and dishes with game.

Hazelnuts.about: Wild hazels grow in hedgerows and woods across Britain, and their nuts ripen in early autumn. The kernels have a sweet, buttery flavour that deepens when toasted. Squirrels often take them before they are ripe, so foragers have to be quick.
Hazelnuts.choose: Choose nuts with full, heavy shells and no holes or cracks, which suggest insects or empty kernels.
Hazelnuts.store: Store in a cool, dry place in their shells for several months, or keep shelled nuts in an airtight jar.
Hazelnuts.prep: Toast to bring out the flavour and loosen the skins, then use in salads, baking, praline or with game and fish.

Wet walnuts.about: Fresh walnuts harvested in early autumn and sold before drying. Their kernels are creamy and mild, with only a hint of the bitterness of dried walnuts. They are a short-season treat, sold for only a few weeks in September and October, and are best peeled before eating.
Wet walnuts.choose: Choose nuts that feel heavy and have clean, unbroken shells with no sign of mould.
Wet walnuts.store: Store in the fridge for up to two weeks, as they spoil faster than dried walnuts.
Wet walnuts.prep: Crack the shells and peel off the bitter skin, then eat with cheese and wine, or use in salads and sauces.

Sweet chestnuts.about: The nuts of the sweet chestnut tree, which grows widely across southern England, ripen in October. They have a floury texture and sweet, nutty flavour, and roasting them is a winter tradition. They are good in stuffings and soups and with sprouts at Christmas.
Sweet chestnuts.choose: Choose shiny, heavy nuts with no holes or mould, and avoid any that rattle in the shell.
Sweet chestnuts.store: Store in a cool, dry place for a week or in the fridge for up to three weeks.
Sweet chestnuts.prep: Score each nut with a cross and roast or boil, then peel while warm; use in stuffings, soups or with Brussels sprouts.
Sweet chestnuts.caution: If foraging, don't confuse sweet chestnuts (spiky, needle-covered cases holding several flattish nuts) with poisonous horse chestnuts or conkers (thick, sparsely spiked cases holding one round nut), and always score before roasting so they don't burst.
